Taught postgraduate: reviews of key texts on programme reading lists. PGR: published book reviews are a common early publication, and venue conventions and editors' expectations are the priority.
reviewNotes: Tagged EGAP because its features are shared across fields, but book reviews are concentrated in the humanities and social sciences and rare in science and engineering coursework; designers may treat it as ESAP for those programmes.

guidance.summary: Reflective writing draws on Schön's (1983) account of the reflective practitioner and is commonly scaffolded with models such as Gibbs's (1988) reflective cycle. Moon (2004) distinguishes descriptive writing from progressively deeper levels of reflection, which helps make markers' expectations explicit. Ryan (2011) argues that reflective writing must be taught as an academic genre with specific linguistic resources, for example the shift from past-tense reporting to present-tense reasoning and future-oriented reconstruction, rather than assumed to come naturally. Because reflective conventions range from personal journals to formal assignments with citations, the brief and local exemplars must guide the form.

activities.title: Depth ladder
learnerActions: Read four extracts reflecting on the same incident at different depths
Rank them and agree what distinguishes each level
Highlight language that signals analysis ('this may have been because', 'in light of')
Rewrite a descriptive extract so that it reaches the next level
activities.intendedInsight: Depth comes from interpretation, questioning and links to theory, not from more detail or stronger emotion.
activities.rationale: Based on Moon's (2004) distinction between descriptive writing and deeper levels of reflection; it makes tacit criteria visible.

activities.title: Mapping reflective language by stage
learnerActions: Analyse a model reflection and label its reporting and responding, relating, reasoning and reconstructing stages
Note tense, pronoun and modal choices in each stage
Draft your own reflection stage by stage with a language bank
Peer-check that each stage does its job
activities.intendedInsight: Each reflective stage has typical language; reflection is a learnable academic genre.
activities.rationale: Applies Ryan's (2011) social semiotic account of reflective writing and its 4Rs scaffold.

difficulties.pattern: 'Reflection is just describing what happened and how I felt.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Narrative-dominated texts with little analysis; feelings reported without interpretation.
difficulties.response: Use word budgets per stage and the depth ladder. Do not respond by discouraging feelings altogether: feelings are data to be analysed.

difficulties.pattern: Discomfort with the first person and with personal disclosure in assessed writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Impersonal reflections that avoid 'I', or, conversely, disclosure beyond what the task needs.
difficulties.response: Explain that the first person is expected here and that 'never use I' is not a rule of academic writing; discuss what to disclose, and how to protect privacy and confidentiality.

difficulties.pattern: Mechanical use of a reflective cycle as a set of headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Six headings with one short paragraph each and a superficial action plan.
difficulties.response: Present models as thinking tools, compare formulaic and integrated reflections, and check the brief on whether headings are expected.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to spend ten minutes reflecting in writing on a recent learning experience in the course.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Brief description, analysis with reasons, a link to a concept or source, and a specific future action.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some analysis but no link to theory, or a vague action ('I will work harder').

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: reflective learning logs and reflections on progress build the genre's language. In-sessional undergraduate: reflective assignments in education, nursing, business and engineering placements, where models and criteria differ. Taught postgraduate: reflective components of professional master's programmes usually require explicit links to theory; see also the professional practice portfolio.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with dhl.reflective-practice (health-specific) and lrn.reflective-logs; this topic covers the general assessed genre.

guidance.summary: Horowitz (1986) found annotated bibliographies among the writing tasks university teachers actually set, and Gardner and Nesi (2013) place them in the Literature Survey family, whose purpose is building research skills. The genre is a useful scaffold because it isolates three skills (summarising, evaluating and judging relevance) that literature reviews later integrate. Briefs vary considerably (descriptive or evaluative annotations, word limits, ordering), so analyse the local brief first. Johns and Mayes (1990) found that less proficient summarisers relied more heavily on copying from the source, a risk that is acute when annotations are written from abstracts.

activities.title: Three-layer annotation
learnerActions: Read an article and write one sentence on its purpose and approach and two on its findings
Add one or two evaluative sentences that use explicit criteria
Add one sentence on relevance to your project
Colour-code the three layers and check that the evaluation is not disguised description
activities.intendedInsight: Annotations combine summary, evaluation and relevance, each with its own language.
activities.rationale: Separating the layers mirrors the main variations in annotated-bibliography briefs and prepares for later synthesis in literature reviews (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: An abstract is not an annotation
learnerActions: Compare a source's abstract with a model annotation of the same source
Identify what the annotation adds and what it leaves out
Rewrite an annotation that was copied from an abstract
activities.intendedInsight: Annotations are written for a different purpose and reader from an abstract.
activities.rationale: Targets the reliance on source wording that Johns and Mayes (1990) observed in less proficient summary writers.

difficulties.pattern: Annotations that paraphrase the abstract.
difficulties.revealedBy: Close textual similarity to abstracts; no evaluation or relevance comment.
difficulties.response: Ask for annotations written from notes on the full text, and show that evaluation and relevance require the writer's own judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluation based on surface features ('a good article because it is recent and long').
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic evaluative comments that could apply to any source.
difficulties.response: Provide evaluation criteria tied to source type, such as sample and design for empirical studies or scope and currency for reviews.

diagnostic.task: Give learners an annotation containing summary, evaluation and relevance sentences and ask them to label each sentence's function.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels every sentence correctly and comments on the adequacy of the evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the summary but confuses evaluation with relevance.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: annotated bibliographies scaffold extended projects. In-sessional undergraduate: often a preparatory assessment before a dissertation or major essay. Taught postgraduate: used as a staged assessment before literature reviews, with higher expectations of evaluation.

guidance.summary: Feak and Swales (2009) present the literature review as telling a research story, with attention to organisation, citation choices and the writer's stance towards the literature. Wallace and Wray (2016) provide a framework for critical engagement with literature that makes evaluation explicit. Coursework literature reviews belong to Gardner and Nesi's (2013) Literature Survey family, whose purpose is building research skills; they differ from review sections in research articles and theses (res.literature-review) because the gap often serves a coursework question rather than justifying the writer's own study. Emphasise synthesis over serial summary, and analyse local exemplars, because expectations range from narrative reviews to systematic-style reviews with documented searches.

activities.title: From list to synthesis
learnerActions: Read a source-by-source review extract
Use a synthesis matrix to regroup its sources by theme
Rewrite one paragraph led by a thematic topic sentence in your own voice, with sources in dialogue
Compare the two versions for voice and evaluation
activities.intendedInsight: Reviews are organised by ideas, and sources serve the writer's points.
activities.rationale: Targets the serial-summary pattern and the questions of organisation and stance discussed by Feak and Swales (2009).

activities.title: Critical questions for the review
learnerActions: For your review question, list what is known, how it is known and what is disputed
Apply critical questions about claims, evidence and warrants to three key sources
Write a paragraph that evaluates the evidence base for one theme
activities.intendedInsight: A literature review evaluates the evidence base rather than simply reporting it.
activities.rationale: Uses Wallace and Wray's (2016) critical reading framework as a writing scaffold.

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source summaries ('Smith (2019) found ... Jones (2020) argued ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs beginning with author names; few comparative or evaluative statements.
difficulties.response: Require thematic topic sentences in the writer's voice and use synthesis matrices. Do not ban integral citation; teach when author prominence is rhetorically useful.

difficulties.pattern: Unsupported or absolute gap claims ('no research has been done on this').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged gap statements, or gaps unrelated to the literature reviewed.
difficulties.response: Teach hedged gap language and require that every gap claim follows from the reviewed literature.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about what to include and how much is enough.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-inclusive reviews that cover everything found; anxiety about missing sources.
difficulties.response: Agree scope criteria tied to the question and keep a search record; explain that coverage depends on the review's purpose.

diagnostic.task: Show two paragraphs reviewing the same three sources, one serial and one synthesised, and ask which is stronger and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Prefers the synthesised paragraph and explains its use of voice, comparison and evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Prefers the synthesised paragraph but cannot say why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Prefers the serial version as clearer.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: short literature reviews within extended projects, often with provided sources. In-sessional undergraduate: reviews in second and final years, frequently preparing for dissertations. Taught postgraduate: stand-alone reviews and dissertation review chapters, with rising expectations of critical evaluation and justified scope.

guidance.summary: Horowitz (1986) found summary of, and reaction to, reading among the tasks university teachers set, and Hirvela (2004) argues that connecting reading and writing, with summary and response at its centre, is fundamental to L2 writing instruction. Leki and Carson (1997) contrasted EAP writing that could draw on personal knowledge with content-course writing that held students responsible for source texts; summary–response builds that text-responsible stance. Grabe and Zhang (2013) argue that reading and writing should be taught together, with explicit attention to summarising and responding.

activities.title: Two-colour paper
learnerActions: Read a model summary–response
Highlight summary sentences in one colour and response sentences in another
Note the signal phrases and reporting verbs at the boundary
Find any sentence that mixes the two and rewrite it
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need to know whose idea is whose, and the boundary is marked linguistically.
activities.rationale: Makes visible the text-responsible stance described by Leki and Carson (1997).

activities.title: Respond to a claim, not a topic
learnerActions: Identify the source's three main claims
Choose one and draft agree, disagree and qualify responses, each with a reason
Select the strongest and develop it with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A response must engage the source's argument rather than the general topic.
activities.rationale: Applies the reading–writing integration Hirvela (2004) advocates.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluation leaking into the summary ('The author wrongly claims ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Loaded reporting verbs and evaluative adjectives in the summary section.
difficulties.response: Contrast neutral and evaluative reporting verbs and reserve evaluation for the response.

difficulties.pattern: The response addresses the general topic rather than the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion essays only loosely connected to the source's argument.
difficulties.response: Require the response to quote or paraphrase the specific claim it answers.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to write a three-sentence summary and a two-sentence response to a short argumentative paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate, attributed summary and a response that engages a specific claim with a reason.
diagnostic.partialResponse: An accurate summary followed by a generic response.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies the source, or gives an opinion without a summary.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: a key entry genre into source-based writing. Pre-sessional: frequent in early weeks and closely related to integrated reading-into-writing tasks. In-sessional undergraduate: appears as reading responses and seminar papers, particularly in the humanities and social sciences.
reviewNotes: The summary–response paper is mainly a North American composition genre; in UK contexts it is more often an EAP or foundation teaching genre than a departmental assessment.

proposedReferences.apa: Horowitz, D. (1986). Essay examination prompts and the teaching of academic writing. *English for Specific Purposes, 5*(2), 107–120.
proposedReferences.note: High confidence in author, year, title and journal; moderate confidence in volume, issue and page range, which should be checked. No DOI given because I am not certain of it. Cited for the general claim that exam essay prompts ask students to select and organise known content in response to specific demands.

authorNotes: ess.essay-types (Essay Construction) overlaps substantially with the GES essay genres (argumentative, discussion, compare-and-contrast, explanation, problem–solution). Suggest scoping ess.essay-types as a brief conceptual overview that these genre topics may take as a soft prerequisite, or retiring it in favour of ges.genre-families.

ges.genre-concept overlaps with acu.discourse-communities. I have not linked them to avoid a potential cross-strand cycle; whichever strand links them should choose one direction (suggested: acu.discourse-communities as a soft prerequisite of ges.genre-concept).
ges.exam-essay overlaps with exm.timed-writing; the latter should remain the generic procedure and the former the genre, which is how they are linked here.

ges.literature-review-assignment and res.literature-review are appropriately split (coursework versus research writing); the research strand already links res.literature-review to this topic, which is the right direction.

ges.reflective-writing overlaps with dhl.reflective-practice and lrn.reflective-logs; dhl.reflective-practice already takes it as a prerequisite. lrn.reflective-logs is not linked to reflective writing to avoid presuming the learning strand's direction.
ges.summary-response is largely a North American composition genre; in UK contexts it is mainly an EAP or foundation teaching genre. Consider noting this in the skeleton scope.

The compare-and-contrast, explanation and problem–solution essays are partly 'cognitive genres' (in Bruce's sense) rather than distinct social genres; they are valid EAP teaching genres but departments rarely name them. A future revision could fold them into one topic on essay rhetorical patterns.
